(CNN) -- Nicaragua President Daniel Ortega said Thursday that the nation is breaking relations with Colombia "in solidarity with the Ecuadoran people." Since that attack, Ecuador has broken off relations with Colombia, and Venezuela says it has moved troops to its border with Colombia. Ortega made his televised remarks in Managua, where he was flanked by Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa. Colombian forces killed at least 17 members of the leftist group Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia on Saturday. FARC is estimated to be holding at least 700 hostages in the jungles of Colombia and has been accused by the United States of being a terrorist organization. "This rupture of relations isn't with the people of Colombia," Ortega said. "We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing." In its resolution, the OAS called the attack "a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law." It ordered a commission, headed by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and composed of four ambassadors designated by him, to visit both countries to investigate the matter, "and to propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together." Colombian officials have apologized for taking their attack against the leftist Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia into Ecuador but said it was necessary to counter a threat to their national security. Colombian officials also said they discovered evidence after the attack that Ecuadoran and Venezuelan government officials were collaborating with the group -- namely that Chavez allegedly gave $300 million to the rebels and that a senior Ecuadoran official met with them. "[They] are making things up and there's no limit to what they'll make up," Chavez said at a news conference on Wednesday. Correa has said his country would only be satisfied when the OAS issues a "clear condemnation" against Colombia for the raid. OAS foreign ministers are to meet March 17 in Washington "to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations," the resolution concluded. The decision follows a resolution passed on Wednesday by the Organization of American States (OAS), which sought to ease the tensions arising from an attack carried out by the Colombian military on a rebel camp in neighboring Ecuador on Saturday. In the wake of that attack, Ecuador has broken off relations with Colombia, while Venezuela reports that it has deployed troops to its border with Colombia.

Ortega delivered his televised remarks in Managua, where he was accompanied by Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa. On Saturday, Colombian forces killed at least 17 members of the leftist group known as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). The organization is believed to be holding at least 700 hostages in the Colombian jungles and has been designated a terrorist organization by the United States.

"This rupture of relations isn't with the people of Colombia," Ortega stated. "We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing."

In its resolution, the OAS characterized the attack as "a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law." It mandated the establishment of a commission—headed by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and comprising four ambassadors of his designation—to visit both nations, investigate the matter, "and to propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together."

Colombian officials have offered an apology for extending their offensive against the leftist Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia into Ecuadoran territory, though they maintained that the operation was necessary to counter a threat to their national security. They further asserted that, following the attack, they had uncovered evidence indicating that Ecuadoran and Venezuelan government officials were collaborating with the group—specifically, that President Chavez had allegedly provided $300 million to the rebels and that a senior Ecuadoran official had met with them.

"[They] are making things up, and there's no limit to what they'll make up," Chavez declared at a news conference on Wednesday.

Correa has stated that his country would be satisfied only when the OAS issues a "clear condemnation" of Colombia for the raid. According to the resolution, OAS foreign ministers are scheduled to convene on March 17 in Washington "to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations."

**MANAGUA, Nicaragua** — Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced Monday that his government is breaking diplomatic relations with Colombia, deepening a regional crisis sparked by a Colombian military raid into neighboring Ecuador that killed a senior FARC guerrilla commander.

Ortega made the announcement during a public speech, expressing solidarity with Ecuador and condemning what he characterized as a violation of national sovereignty in the region.

"We cannot maintain relations with a government that has taken these kinds of actions," Ortega declared, calling the cross-border operation an affront to Latin American principles of non-intervention.

## Regional Tensions Escalate

The diplomatic rupture follows the March 1 Colombian raid that killed Raúl Reyes, a top commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), inside Ecuadorean territory. The operation has ignited one of the most serious diplomatic confrontations in the region in years.

Ecuador and Venezuela had already moved troops toward their borders with Colombia and expelled Colombian diplomats in the days following the incident. Nicaragua's decision adds another voice to the chorus of nations criticizing Bogotá.

## Colombia Defends Its Actions

Colombian President Álvaro Uribe's government has defended the raid as a legitimate action against a terrorist organization responsible for decades of violence, kidnappings, and drug trafficking.

Colombian officials have pointed to documents allegedly recovered from the camp, which they claim reveal ties between the FARC and neighboring governments — accusations that have further inflamed tensions across the region.

## Ortega's Broader Grievances

Ortega, a former Sandinista revolutionary with longstanding ideological differences with the conservative Uribe administration, also referenced an unrelated territorial dispute between the two nations over islands in the Caribbean Sea.

The Nicaraguan leader aligned himself with Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez and Ecuadorean President Rafael Correa, both vocal critics of Colombia's actions and its close alliance with the United States.

## Calls for De-escalation

The crisis has drawn concern from across the international community, with regional bodies and outside nations urging restraint. The Organization of American States has faced pressure to mediate the growing dispute.

Analysts warn that the confrontation risks destabilizing an already tense region, though most observers believe full-scale armed conflict remains unlikely.

**BOGOTÁ/QUITO/CARACAS** — A major diplomatic crisis has engulfed South America after Colombian military forces conducted a cross-border raid into Ecuadorian territory, killing senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and roughly two dozen others at a guerrilla encampment.

**President Rafael Correa** reacted with outrage, denouncing the incursion as a flagrant violation of Ecuadorian sovereignty and international law. Correa announced the withdrawal of Ecuador's ambassador from Bogotá and moved troops toward the northern border.

"This is an aggression against our territory," Correa declared, rejecting Colombia's justifications and demanding a formal apology. He embarked on a regional tour to rally support from Latin American leaders.

**Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez** delivered some of the most forceful rhetoric, ordering troops and tanks to the Colombian border and closing Venezuela's embassy in Bogotá.

"This could be the start of a war in South America," Chávez warned during his televised address, cautioning Colombia against attempting a similar operation on Venezuelan soil. He described Uribe as a servant of foreign interests and honored the slain FARC commander during his broadcast.

"We are breaking relations with Colombia in solidarity with the Ecuadorian people," Ortega said, condemning what he called an act of aggression and terrorism by the Colombian state.

The **Organization of American States (OAS)** called an emergency meeting of its Permanent Council to address the escalating crisis. Secretary General José Miguel Insulza urged restraint from all parties and emphasized the principle of territorial inviolability enshrined in the OAS charter.

Diplomats worked to craft a resolution that would acknowledge the violation of Ecuadorian sovereignty while seeking to prevent the confrontation from escalating into broader armed conflict. Regional bodies signaled a preference for a diplomatic resolution.

The crisis underscores deep ideological divisions in the region, pitting Colombia's U.S.-aligned government against the left-leaning administrations of Venezuela, Ecuador, and Nicaragua. # OAS Condemns Colombian Raid into Ecuadoran Territory as Regional Tensions Escalate

**Diplomatic crisis deepens across South America following cross-border military operation**

WASHINGTON — The Organization of American States (OAS) approved a resolution condemning Colombia's military incursion into Ecuadoran territory, marking a significant diplomatic rebuke as the raid ignited one of the most serious regional crises South America has faced in recent years.

The resolution, adopted after intense negotiations among member states, characterized the Colombian operation as a violation of Ecuador's sovereignty and territorial integrity—principles enshrined in international law and the founding charter of the hemispheric body.

## The Incursion

The crisis erupted when Colombian security forces crossed into Ecuadoran territory in a military operation targeting a camp belonging to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the leftist guerrilla group that has waged a decades-long insurgency against the Colombian government. The raid resulted in the death of a senior FARC commander along with other members of the organization.

Colombian officials defended the operation as a legitimate action against a terrorist group that had established a base of operations across the border. Bogotá maintained that the strike was necessary to protect national security and combat an armed group responsible for kidnappings, drug trafficking, and violence within Colombia.

## Ecuador's Response

Ecuador reacted with fury to the violation of its territory, denouncing the incursion as an act of aggression that trampled on its national sovereignty. Quito recalled its ambassador from Bogotá and moved troops toward its northern border with Colombia, dramatically raising the stakes in an already volatile situation.

Ecuadoran authorities rejected Colombia's justifications, arguing that no nation has the right to unilaterally violate the borders of a sovereign neighbor, regardless of the target. The government emphasized that legitimate concerns about armed groups should be addressed through diplomatic channels and bilateral cooperation rather than unilateral military action.

## Regional Fallout

The crisis quickly spread beyond the two directly involved nations, drawing in other regional powers and threatening to destabilize relations across the continent. Venezuela, under a government sympathetic to Ecuador's position, condemned the Colombian action in strong terms and took its own measures signaling displeasure with Bogotá, further inflaming tensions.

The confrontation exposed deep ideological divisions in South America, pitting governments aligned along different political lines against one another. Diplomatic relations between several nations frayed as leaders exchanged accusations and warnings, raising fears of a broader regional confrontation.

## The OAS Deliberations

Against this backdrop of escalating tension, the OAS convened to address the crisis. Diplomats engaged in prolonged negotiations to craft language that would acknowledge the violation of Ecuadoran sovereignty while leaving room for eventual reconciliation between the parties.

The resulting resolution reaffirmed the fundamental principle that the territory of a state is inviolable and may not be the object of military occupation or other measures of force taken by another state. While condemning the incursion, the body also called for dialogue and the peaceful resolution of the dispute, seeking to prevent further deterioration.

The measure represented a diplomatic compromise, as some nations pushed for stronger condemnation while others sought to acknowledge Colombia's security concerns regarding armed groups operating near its borders.

## Broader Implications

The episode highlighted the persistent challenges posed by cross-border insurgency and the difficulty of balancing legitimate security concerns against the bedrock principle of national sovereignty. For Colombia, the operation reflected the government's determination to pursue FARC forces wherever they might seek refuge. For Ecuador and its allies, it represented a dangerous precedent that could not be allowed to stand.

Analysts noted that the crisis underscored the fragility of regional stability and the potential for localized conflicts to rapidly escalate into wider diplomatic confrontations. The role of the OAS in mediating the dispute demonstrated the continued relevance of multilateral institutions in managing tensions among member states.

## Path Forward

In the wake of the resolution, attention turned to whether the affected nations could repair their damaged relationships and restore normal diplomatic ties. Regional leaders and international observers called for restraint and urged the parties to pursue reconciliation through established diplomatic mechanisms.

The crisis served as a stark reminder of the volatile intersection between internal armed conflicts and international relations in the region, leaving lasting questions about sovereignty, security cooperation, and the mechanisms available to resolve disputes among neighbors.

As the dust settled on the immediate confrontation, the long-term consequences for regional cooperation and the precedent set by the incursion remained subjects of intense debate throughout the hemisphere.

The operation targeted a camp of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) situated approximately 1.8 kilometers inside Ecuador's border. Colombian officials suggested that documents recovered from the camp contained information about FARC ties to regional governments—claims that further inflamed tensions with neighbors.

## International Response

The crisis drew attention across the hemisphere, with the Organization of American States (OAS) becoming a focal point for diplomatic efforts to defuse the situation. Regional leaders called for restraint and dialogue to prevent further escalation between the involved parties.

The episode highlighted the complex challenges posed by the FARC insurgency spilling across borders, as well as the deep political divisions among Andean nations. It underscored tensions between the imperative to combat armed groups and the principle of respecting national sovereignty—a balance that continues to challenge regional diplomacy.
